relations.myth: Manu establishes Agni as humanity’s ritual light
relations.note: Manu establishes or kindles Agni as the ritual light of human communities.

relations.myth: Agni performs sacrifice among Manu’s descendants
relations.note: Agni dwells among Manu’s people and performs the sacrifice modeled on Manu’s precedent.

relations.myth: Mātariśvan conveys Agni to Manu
relations.note: Mātariśvan gives or conveys the divine fire Agni to Manu.

relations.myth: Indra drinks pressed Soma with Manu
relations.note: Indra drinks Soma together with Manu Vivasvat or Manu Sāṃvaraṇi.

relations.myth: Manu’s Soma empowers Indra against Vṛtra
relations.note: Indra drinks Manu’s Soma before undertaking his battle against Vṛtra.

relations.myth: Soma flows for Manu’s primordial offering
relations.note: Soma flows for Manu or is offered by him as ritual precedent.

relations.myth: Śyena brings Soma to Manu
relations.note: The divine bird brings the sacred Soma to Manu.

relations.myth: Rudra invoked through Father Manu’s good fortune
relations.note: Worshippers ask Rudra to grant the prosperity and longevity Father Manu obtained through sacrifice.

relations.myth: Ādityas invoked through Manu’s first sacrifice
relations.note: The Ādityas are asked to grant the safety associated with Manu’s primordial sacrifice.

relations.myth: Manu protects the growing fish
relations.note: Manu rears and protects the small fish as it grows.

relations.myth: The fish saves Manu from the flood
relations.note: The fish warns Manu, directs his shipbuilding, and tows his vessel to safety.

relations.myth: Idā arises from Manu’s post-flood offering
relations.note: Manu’s water-offering generates Idā, who becomes the blessing of his regenerative sacrifice.

relations.myth: Idā identifies herself as Manu’s daughter
relations.note: The woman generated from Manu’s offering explicitly identifies herself as his daughter.

relations.myth: Brahmā as fish saves Manu’s ship
relations.note: The rescuing fish reveals itself as Brahmā after towing Manu through the deluge.

relations.myth: Brahmā commands Manu to recreate beings
relations.note: After the flood, Brahmā commissions Manu to regenerate the world through ascetic power.

relations.myth: Seven seers accompany Manu through the flood
relations.note: The seven seers join Manu aboard the seed-bearing ship during the epic deluge.

relations.myth: Manu recreates beings after the flood
relations.note: Manu recreates the gods and other beings through ascetic power after the deluge.

relations.myth: Manu recreates beings after the flood
relations.note: Manu recreates the Asuras and other beings through ascetic power after the deluge.

relations.myth: Matsya saves Manu from cosmic dissolution
relations.note: Viṣṇu’s fish incarnation guides Manu’s vessel safely through the cosmic flood.

relations.myth: Matsya teaches Manu during Brahmā’s night
relations.note: Matsya instructs Manu in supreme knowledge while towing the flood vessel.

relations.myth: Vāsuki fastens Manu’s boat to Matsya
relations.note: Vāsuki serves as the rope binding Manu’s vessel to Matsya’s horn.
Later solar genealogies identify Vaivasvata Manu as the son of Vivasvat.

relations.myth: Vivasvat transmits Kṛṣṇa’s yoga to Manu
relations.note: Vivasvat teaches Manu the imperishable yoga that he previously received from Kṛṣṇa.
Later genealogies make Saraṇyū, also called Saṃjñā, the mother of Vaivasvata Manu.
Solar genealogies make Yama the brother or half-brother of Vaivasvata Manu.
Later solar genealogies make Yamī the sister or half-sister of Vaivasvata Manu.
Some genealogies make the Aśvins brothers or half-brothers of Manu through Saraṇyū.
Some genealogical arrangements make Sāvarṇi the half-brother of Vaivasvata Manu.
Several later accounts identify Śraddhā as Vaivasvata Manu’s wife or ritual partner.
Vaivasvata Manu fathers Ikṣvāku, founder of the Solar Dynasty’s principal royal line.
Nabhāga appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.
Dhṛṣṭa appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.
Śaryāti appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.
Nariṣyanta appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.
Nābhāganediṣṭha is Manu’s son, with traditions varying over his name and inheritance.
Karūṣa appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.
Pṛṣadhra appears among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons in a common Purāṇic genealogy.
Some Purāṇic lists name Prāṃśu as one of Vaivasvata Manu’s sons.
Some Purāṇic lists substitute Vasumat among Vaivasvata Manu’s sons.
Later genealogies make Ilā or Sudyumna Manu’s child, with sex and birth varying by account.
Manu is Purūravas’s ancestor through Manu’s child Ilā and Ilā’s union with Budha.
Royal genealogies make Manu an ancestor of Rāma through Ikṣvāku and the Solar Dynasty.

relations.myth: Brahmā emanates Svāyambhuva Manu
relations.note: Purāṇic creation accounts make Svāyambhuva Manu emerge from Brahmā or the self-existent creator.

relations.myth: Brahmā teaches primordial dharma to Manu
relations.note: The Manusmṛti frame presents Brahmā as teaching the complete knowledge of dharma to Manu.
Later cosmology identifies Śatarūpā as the consort of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Priyavrata is commonly listed as a child of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.
Uttānapāda is commonly listed as a child of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.
Ākūti is commonly listed as a daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.
Devahūti is commonly listed as a daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.
Prasūti is commonly listed as a daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā.

relations.myth: Devī grants Suratha future Manu status
relations.note: Devī grants King Suratha the boon of becoming the future Sāvarṇi Manu.
Genealogies derive Sāvarṇi Manu from Chāyā or Savarṇā, the Sun’s substitute wife.
Variable Purāṇic lists make a future Rudra-Sāvarṇi Manu the son or derivative of Rudra.
Some Purāṇic systems describe Śiva or Rudra as patron of the future Rudra-Sāvarṇi Manu.
